name: Spanning Tree
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Elect the root, assign Rapid PVST+ roles, read show spanning-tree and place PortFast, BPDU guard and filter, root and loop guard.

resources.title: Free CCNA course (Jeremy's IT Lab)

lesson.intro: Redundant links keep a network up when a cable fails, but without spanning tree they bring it down in seconds. Learn which switch becomes root and why, what role each port plays, how PortFast speeds up edge ports, and which guard belongs where.
objectives: Explain the three problems a Layer 2 loop causes and how STP prevents them
Elect the root bridge and choose root, designated and alternate ports by cost
Interpret Rapid PVST+ roles, states and show spanning-tree output
Choose between PortFast, BPDU guard, BPDU filter, root guard and loop guard
Recognize err-disabled and inconsistent ports and recover them correctly

sections.title: Why a loop takes the network down
sections.key: Without STP, redundant links loop frames forever because Ethernet has no TTL; STP blocks just enough ports to leave exactly one active path between any two points.
sections.body:
Three switches cabled in a triangle survive any single link failure. Then a PC sends one ARP broadcast. Each switch floods it, the copies circle in both directions and multiply at every switch, and Ethernet frames have no TTL to stop them. Within seconds the links are saturated.

[[visual]]

**Spanning Tree Protocol** (STP, originally IEEE 802.1D) puts each port in a forwarding or blocking state so that exactly one active path exists between any two points: a loop-free tree. A blocked port stays up and keeps listening to STP messages, so STP can unblock it when an active link fails.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Three problems without STP
rows: Frames are forwarded around the loop again and again, eating every link
Copies arrive from different directions, so switches keep relearning the same source MAC on different ports
Hosts receive several copies of the same frame

visual.title: The triangle becomes a tree
visual.caption: If SW1 to SW2 fails, STP unblocks SW2 Gi0/1 and SW2 reaches the root through SW3.

sections.pitfall: Treating STP as optional because "we have no redundant links". A patch cable between two wall jacks or a cheap unmanaged switch can create a loop in seconds. Never disable spanning tree.

check.question: Why does a broadcast frame circle a switched loop indefinitely, while a looping IP packet eventually dies?
choices: Switches cache broadcasts and resend them every second
IP packets are smaller than Ethernet frames
Ethernet frames have no TTL field; routers decrement the IP TTL until the packet is dropped
TCP retransmits each packet only once
check.explanation: Nothing in an Ethernet header limits how many times a switch can forward a frame. IP's TTL is decremented at every router hop, so a routing loop eventually discards the packet.

sections.title: Electing the root bridge
sections.key: The switch with the lowest bridge ID becomes root: lowest priority first (default 32768, shown plus the VLAN number), then lowest MAC address as the tiebreaker.
sections.body:
STP first picks one reference switch, the **root bridge**. Switches exchange **BPDUs** (bridge protocol data units). Hello BPDUs carry the root's bridge ID, the sender's bridge ID, its cost to the root and timers. Every switch starts by claiming to be root, and stops when it hears a **superior** (lower) root bridge ID.

[[visual]]

Show commands print priority plus VLAN, so a default switch in VLAN 10 shows 32778. Priority is compared first; only on a tie does the lowest MAC win.

[[visual 2]]

Valid priorities are multiples of 4096, from 0 to 61440 (8192 works, 10000 is rejected). To read a shown priority, subtract the VLAN: 24586 in VLAN 10 means 24576.

The election never ends: a switch with a better bridge ID plugged in later takes over, so choose the root on purpose.

visual.title: Who wins VLAN 10?
visual.caption: SW1 wins on priority, so MACs are never compared. If all three were at 32768, SW3 would win with the lowest MAC.

sections.deeper: **Why multiples of 4096?** The priority was originally a 16-bit number (0 to 65535). When per-VLAN trees arrived, the IEEE carved the low 12 bits off for the VLAN ID, leaving 4 bits of real priority. The command still takes the old 16-bit decimal value, so only values whose low 12 bits are zero are legal: 0, 4096, 8192 and so on up to 61440. That is also why the shown value is the configured priority plus the VLAN number.
sections.pitfall: Trying to set a priority that is not a multiple of 4096, such as 10000. IOS rejects it, because the low 12 bits of the field belong to the VLAN ID.

activity.title: Who becomes root?
activity.prompt: Before changing anything, predict the root bridge from the priorities and MAC addresses. Then lower a different switch's priority to 4096 and predict the new root ports and the blocked port before you apply it. Finally, raise the cost of one link and watch which port blocks.

check.question: Three switches use default STP settings in VLAN 1. Which one becomes the root bridge?
choices: The one with the highest MAC address
The one with the most ports
The one that booted first
The one with the lowest MAC address
check.explanation: With equal priorities (32769 in VLAN 1), the lowest MAC address breaks the tie. Boot order and port count do not matter, because the election continues whenever a better BID appears.

sections.title: Choosing the root: primary, secondary, per VLAN
sections.key: root primary sets priority 24576 (or 4096 below the current root), root secondary sets 28672, and per-VLAN roots let both distribution uplinks carry traffic.
sections.body:
Pick the root on purpose, per VLAN:

[[visual]]

Both root commands are one-time macros: the running config stores the resulting `priority` value. One command can cover a list: `spanning-tree vlan 1,10,20 root primary`.

[[visual 2]]

Rapid PVST+ runs a tree per VLAN, so two distribution switches can share the work. DSW1 is primary root for VLANs 10 and 30 and secondary for 20 and 40; DSW2 is the reverse. Each access uplink forwards for half the VLANs, and if either switch fails, the secondary takes over its VLANs.

[[visual 3]]

Rapid PVST+ sends one set of BPDUs per VLAN, inside that VLAN (tagged on trunks), to `0100.0CCC.CCCD`, with the VLAN in the bridge ID's system ID extension. Standard RSTP sends one untagged set to `0180.C200.0000` for all VLANs.

rows: 24576, or 4096 below the current root if that root is already at 24576 or lower
28672: below every default switch, above the primary

visual.title: root primary when SW3 is root at 16384
visual.result: SW1 stores `spanning-tree vlan 20 priority 12288` and becomes root

visual.title: Per-VLAN load sharing
visual.caption: Each uplink forwards for two VLANs and is an alternate (discarding) port for the other two.

sections.code:
! Load sharing between two distribution switches
DSW1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10,30 root primary
DSW1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 20,40 root secondary
DSW2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 20,40 root primary
DSW2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10,30 root secondary

! What DSW1 actually stores
DSW1# show running-config | include spanning-tree vlan
spanning-tree vlan 10,30 priority 24576
spanning-tree vlan 20,40 priority 28672
sections.tip: Exam shortcut: root primary 24576 (or 4096 below the current root), root secondary 28672, default 32768. Add the VLAN number to get what show spanning-tree prints.
sections.pitfall: Expecting root primary to keep tracking the network. It is a one-time calculation stored as a fixed priority; if a switch with 20480 appears later, your "primary" loses.

check.question: SW2 is currently root for VLAN 10 with priority 24576. You enter spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary on SW1. Which priority does SW1 configure?
check.explanation: root primary chooses 24576 unless the current root is already at 24576 or lower; then it picks 4096 less than the current root, here 20480, so SW1 wins outright. 28672 is the root secondary value.

sections.title: Root ports, designated ports and cost
sections.key: Each non-root switch's root port has the lowest root cost, each link's designated port advertises the lowest root cost, and every other port is alternate and discards.
sections.body:
With the root chosen, each port gets a role from its **cost**, set by the speed it runs at:

[[visual]]

The root sends Hellos with a root cost of 0. A switch adds its arrival port's cost to the cost in the Hello; that total is its **root cost** through that port.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

[[visual 4]]

Steer the choice with interface commands: `spanning-tree [vlan 10] cost 2` overrides a port's cost, and `spanning-tree [vlan 10] port-priority 64` changes the tiebreaker neighbors see. Lowering the cost of the preferred path is the usual tool.

visual.title: Default port costs
visual.caption: The short method Cisco uses by default; spanning-tree pathcost method long switches to 32-bit values such as 20,000 for 1 Gbps. A gigabit port running at 100 Mbps costs 19.

visual.title: SW4 picks its root port

steps.label: Gi0/2, via a neighbor 2 hops out
steps.note: received root cost 6, plus port cost 4

visual.result: Gi0/2 is the root port (10 beats 19), even though Fa0/1 is the direct link

visual.title: The three rules
rows: On each non-root switch, the one port with the lowest root cost
Lowest neighbor bridge ID, then lowest neighbor port priority, then lowest neighbor port number
On each link, the port on the switch advertising the lowest root cost; every working port on the root is a DP
Every other port: it discards, a ready backup path to the root

visual.title: The triangle, every link 1 Gbps (cost 4)
visual.caption: On the SW2 to SW3 link both advertise root cost 4. Priorities tie, so SW3's lower MAC wins the designated port and SW2's port discards.

sections.pitfall: Choosing the root port by the cost of the local link alone. Root cost is the whole path: the cost in the received Hello plus the cost of the port it arrived on.

check.question: SW3 can reach the root through Gi0/1 (received root cost 0, port cost 19) or Gi0/2 (received root cost 4, port cost 4). Which is SW3's root port?
choices: Gi0/1, because it connects directly to the root
Gi0/2, with a root cost of 8
Gi0/1, with a root cost of 19
Neither; the paths tie
check.explanation: Gi0/1 totals 0 + 19 = 19, and Gi0/2 totals 4 + 4 = 8. The lower total wins, so Gi0/2 is the root port even though Gi0/1 is the direct link to the root.

sections.title: Rapid PVST+: roles, states and speed
sections.key: Rapid PVST+ runs RSTP per VLAN, with three states (discarding, learning, forwarding) and alternate ports that take over at once, converging in about a second.
sections.body:
Classic 802.1D was slow. After losing Hellos it waited **MaxAge** (20 seconds), then the **forward delay** (15 seconds) listening and 15 more learning: up to 50 seconds of outage.

**Rapid STP** (RSTP, 802.1w) keeps the same election but converges in a second or two. Neighbors agree on roles with a proposal and agreement handshake instead of timers, and a neighbor is lost after three missed Hellos (sent every 2 seconds).

When a root port fails, the **alternate port** becomes the root port and forwards at once, because it already hears the same root.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Cisco runs one tree **per VLAN**, and the CCNA expects Rapid PVST+ (`spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst`):

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Roles and link types
rows: Best path from a non-root switch to the root
The forwarding port for a link
Discarding backup path to the root through another switch
Backup for a designated port on the same shared segment (hubs only, rare)
A port that is administratively down
Full duplex: the normal switch-to-switch case
A PortFast port facing an end device

visual.title: spanning-tree mode
rows: One per instance, each holding many VLANs

sections.deeper: **When the topology changes.** If a new link comes up between two switches, the designated side sends a proposal, the other side briefly blocks its other non-edge ports and answers with an agreement, and the link forwards in well under a second. Whenever a switch changes the topology it sends a topology change notice, so other switches flush the MAC addresses learned on affected ports and relearn them on the new path. Edge (PortFast) ports going up and down cause no topology change at all, one more reason to configure PortFast on every end-device port.
sections.pitfall: Confusing alternate and backup ports. Alternate: a different path to the root, the one you meet constantly. Backup: a second port on the same shared segment, which only happens with hubs.

check.question: In Rapid PVST+, a port receives Hellos from the root bridge but offers a worse path than the root port, so it is discarding. What is its role?
choices: Alternate
Backup
Designated
Disabled
check.explanation: An alternate port is a backup path to the root through another switch, kept discarding until the root port fails. A backup port backs up a designated port on a shared segment.

sections.title: Reading show spanning-tree
sections.key: show spanning-tree vlan 10 shows the root's ID, this switch's own bridge ID, and each port's role, state, cost, priority and type; the root says This bridge is the root.
sections.body:
`show spanning-tree vlan 10` answers nearly every STP question in three blocks:

[[code]]

[[visual]]

In the exhibit SW2 is not the root. The root shows 24586 (24576 plus VLAN 10) at SW1's MAC, and SW2 reaches it with cost 4 through Gi0/2, its root port. Gi0/1 is the alternate port (BLK), and Fa0/11 is an Edge port, so PortFast is on.

In a multi-switch exhibit, the root is the switch whose Root ID matches its own Bridge ID.

rows: The root's priority and MAC. On a non-root switch, also this switch's root cost and root port. On the root: This bridge is the root
This switch's priority (the total, then priority plus sys-id-ext) and its MAC
FWD, LRN, or BLK for discarding
P2p or Shr, plus Edge for PortFast ports

sections.code:
SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 10

VLAN0010
  Spanning tree enabled protocol rstp
  Root ID    Priority    24586
             Address     0019.e859.5380
             Cost        4
             Port        26 (GigabitEthernet0/2)

  Bridge ID  Priority    32778  (priority 32768 sys-id-ext 10)
             Address     0019.e86a.6f80
! timers omitted

Interface           Role Sts Cost      Prio.Nbr Type
------------------- ---- --- --------- -------- --------------------------------
Gi0/1               Altn BLK 4         128.25   P2p
Gi0/2               Root FWD 4         128.26   P2p
Fa0/11              Desg FWD 19        128.11   P2p Edge
sections.pitfall: Reading BLK in Rapid PVST+ output as the old 802.1D blocking state. IOS still prints BLK for a discarding port; the Role column (Altn or Back) tells you why it discards.

check.question: show spanning-tree vlan 10 on a switch says 'This bridge is the root'. What role do this switch's working ports have in VLAN 10?
choices: Root
Alternate
Designated
Backup
check.explanation: The root bridge has no root port; every working port on it is designated and forwarding. Root ports exist only on non-root switches.

sections.title: PortFast: edge ports skip the wait
sections.key: PortFast puts a port facing a single end device straight into forwarding as an edge port; it is a speed feature, so pair it with BPDU guard.
sections.body:
A user plugs in a laptop. With classic 802.1D the port spends 30 seconds listening and learning, long enough for the laptop's DHCP request to time out. A port to one end device cannot create a loop, so the wait is pointless.

**PortFast** moves the port straight to forwarding when the link comes up. In Rapid PVST+ it is an **edge port** (Type shows Edge). If an edge port ever receives a BPDU, it loses edge status and runs normal STP.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Configuring a voice VLAN on a Catalyst port turns PortFast on automatically, since a phone is an end device.

rows: PortFast on every port operating as an access port
Exempts one port from the default
PortFast on a trunk to a server or a router on a stick
The same as portfast, on newer IOS

sections.code:
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/11
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
%Warning: portfast should only be enabled on ports connected to a single
 host. Connecting hubs, concentrators, switches, bridges, etc... to this
 interface  when portfast is enabled, can cause temporary bridging loops.
 Use with CAUTION

! Or for every access port at once:
SW1(config)# spanning-tree portfast default
sections.pitfall: Enabling PortFast on a link to another switch. You skip the checks that prevent loops; keep PortFast for end devices (and the special trunk case of servers and routers).

check.question: What does PortFast change on an access port?
choices: It disables spanning tree on the port completely
It moves the port to forwarding immediately instead of waiting through listening and learning
It raises the port to its maximum speed
It makes the port the switch's root port
check.explanation: PortFast skips the transitional states so the end device gets connectivity at once. STP still runs on the port: if a BPDU arrives, the port stops being an edge port.

sections.title: BPDU guard and BPDU filter
sections.key: BPDU guard err-disables a PortFast port the moment a BPDU arrives; interface BPDU filter instead ignores BPDUs, which silently turns STP off on that port.
sections.body:
End devices never send BPDUs. A BPDU on a PortFast port means someone plugged in a switch: a user's cheap switch that could loop, or an attacker with a low priority trying to become root and see traffic.

**BPDU guard** puts the port in the **err-disabled** state on the first BPDU:

[[visual]]

Enable it per interface with `spanning-tree bpduguard enable`, or on every PortFast port with `spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default`. `errdisable recovery cause bpduguard` retries automatically, after 300 seconds by default. Never use it toward another switch: that switch's BPDUs err-disable the uplink at once.

**BPDU filter** suppresses BPDUs, in two very different forms:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

visual.title: A user plugs in a small switch

items.title: Global form
points: PortFast ports stop sending BPDUs after a few at link-up
A received BPDU removes PortFast and filtering: normal STP resumes

items.title: Interface form
points: The port neither sends nor processes BPDUs
Plug in a switch and you can build a loop STP cannot see
Use rarely, where BPDUs must not be sent

sections.code:
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# spanning-tree portfast
SW1(config-if-range)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable

! Later, a switch is plugged into Fa0/5:
%SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD: Received BPDU on port Fa0/5 with BPDU Guard enabled. Disabling port.
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Fa0/5, putting Fa0/5 in err-disable state
sections.pitfall: Enabling interface BPDU filter on user ports to stop BPDU guard shutting them down. It removes loop protection entirely. Find and remove the device sending BPDUs instead.

activity.title: Set the root and harden an edge port
activity.prompt: Make SW1 the primary root for VLANs 1, 10 and 20 with a single command, then enable PortFast and BPDU guard on access port G0/1. Afterward, run show spanning-tree vlan 10 and predict the Bridge ID priority before you look: why should it be 24586 rather than 24576?

check.question: A user plugs a small switch into an access port configured with PortFast and BPDU guard. The small switch sends BPDUs. What happens?
choices: The small switch becomes the root bridge
The port loses PortFast but keeps forwarding
The BPDUs are silently dropped and the port keeps forwarding
The access port is err-disabled
check.explanation: BPDU guard err-disables the port on the first BPDU. Without BPDU guard, the port would simply lose edge status and run normal STP; with interface BPDU filter, the BPDUs would be ignored.

sections.title: Root guard and loop guard
sections.key: Root guard blocks a designated port that hears a superior BPDU; loop guard blocks a root or alternate port whose BPDUs stop; both recover on their own.
sections.body:
Two more features protect the shape of the tree.

**Root guard** (`spanning-tree guard root`) goes on **designated ports** facing switches that must never become root, such as a distribution switch's downlinks. If a **superior BPDU** arrives, the port goes **root-inconsistent** (discarding) and the real root stays root. It recovers when those BPDUs stop; nothing is err-disabled.

**Loop guard** (`spanning-tree guard loop`, or `spanning-tree loopguard default` globally) protects **root and alternate ports**, which should keep hearing BPDUs. On a **unidirectional link** (one fiber strand failed), an alternate port stops hearing BPDUs and would turn designated and forward, creating a loop. Loop guard makes it **loop-inconsistent** instead, until BPDUs return.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Where each protection goes
visual.caption: Root guard on the distribution downlinks (designated ports), loop guard on ASW1's root port and its alternate (dashed) port, PortFast and BPDU guard toward the PC.

visual.title: The four protections
rows: Err-disable; recover manually or with errdisable recovery
PortFast access ports facing end devices
The port neither sends nor processes BPDUs
Rarely, where BPDUs must not be sent
Designated ports toward switches that must never be root
Root and alternate ports on switch-to-switch links
visual.caption: Root guard and loop guard share the spanning-tree guard command, so a port has one or the other, never both.

sections.pitfall: Putting root guard on a switch's root port. That port hears the real root's superior BPDUs, so root guard would cut the switch off. Use it on designated ports facing downstream.

check.question: A distribution switch should never accept an access switch as the root bridge. Which feature belongs on its downlinks to the access switches?
choices: Loop guard
Root guard
PortFast
BPDU filter
check.explanation: Root guard on those designated ports blocks them (root-inconsistent) if an access switch advertises a superior BPDU, so the intended root keeps its place. Loop guard protects against BPDUs disappearing, not against a better root appearing.

sections.title: Verifying PortFast and the guard features
sections.key: BKN* with ROOT_Inc, LOOP_Inc or PVID_Inc means a port is blocked until its problem clears, while BPDU guard err-disables a port until you bounce it.
sections.body:
Configuring protection is half the job; you also need to recognize it working in exhibits.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Keep the two recovery models straight:

[[visual 2]]

rows: The mode, VLANs this switch is root for, EtherChannel misconfig guard, and the global PortFast, BPDU guard, BPDU filter and loop guard defaults
One port: portfast mode, Bpdu guard, Root guard or Loop guard enabled, and BPDUs sent and received (0 received is right for an edge port)
BKN* in the Sts column, with the reason in Type
Every inconsistent port in one list
Ports shut down by BPDU guard (reason bpduguard) or other causes
Superior BPDU on a root guard port
BPDUs stopped on a loop guard port
The native VLAN differs on the two trunk ends
Any BPDU on a BPDU guard port
shutdown and no shutdown, or errdisable recovery

sections.code:
SW1# show spanning-tree summary
Switch is in rapid-pvst mode
Root bridge for: VLAN0010, VLAN0030
EtherChannel misconfig guard            is enabled
Portfast Default                        is enabled
PortFast BPDU Guard Default             is enabled
Portfast BPDU Filter Default            is disabled
Loopguard Default                       is disabled
! lines omitted

SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10 | begin Interface
Interface           Role Sts Cost      Prio.Nbr Type
------------------- ---- --- --------- -------- --------------------------------
Gi0/1               Desg BKN*4         128.1    P2p *ROOT_Inc
Gi0/2               Desg FWD 4         128.2    P2p
Fa0/11              Desg FWD 19        128.11   P2p Edge
sections.pitfall: Bouncing a root-inconsistent or loop-inconsistent port with shutdown and no shutdown. It is not err-disabled; fix the cause (the rogue root or the one-way link) and it recovers by itself.

check.question: show spanning-tree vlan 10 shows Gi0/1 with Sts BKN* and Type *ROOT_Inc. What happened?
choices: BPDU guard err-disabled the port
Root guard blocked the port because it received a superior BPDU
Loop guard blocked the port because BPDUs stopped arriving
The port is a PortFast edge port waiting to forward
check.explanation: ROOT_Inc means root inconsistent: root guard heard a BPDU claiming a better root on that port and blocks it until those BPDUs stop. Loop guard would show LOOP_Inc, and BPDU guard err-disables the port instead of marking it inconsistent.

keyTerms.definition: The switch with the lowest bridge ID; the reference point of the spanning tree. All its working ports are designated.
8-byte switch identifier: 4-bit priority (multiples of 4096), 12-bit extended system ID (the VLAN) and 48-bit MAC.
Bridge protocol data unit: the STP message carrying root ID, sender ID, root cost and timers.
The total STP cost from a switch to the root: the cost in the received Hello plus the receiving port's cost.
On a non-root switch, the single port with the lowest root cost toward the root bridge.
On each link, the port of the switch advertising the lowest root cost onto that link; it forwards.
An RSTP role: a discarding port that offers a backup path to the root and can take over quickly.
Cisco's per-VLAN version of RSTP (802.1w), set with spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst.
Moves an edge port straight to forwarding; for ports connected to end devices.
Err-disables a port as soon as it receives any BPDU; pairs with PortFast on access ports.
Puts a port in root-inconsistent state if it receives a superior BPDU, protecting the chosen root.
Puts a root or alternate port in loop-inconsistent state if its BPDUs stop, preventing loops from unidirectional links.
The 12 bits of the bridge ID priority field that hold the VLAN number, so shown priority = configured priority + VLAN.
Macros that set priority 24576 (or 4096 below the current root) and 28672; stored as a numeric priority.
Suppresses BPDUs: globally on PortFast ports (reverts on a received BPDU), or per interface where it effectively disables STP.
Blocking state set by root guard while superior BPDUs arrive; shown as *ROOT_Inc and cleared automatically.
Blocking state set by loop guard when expected BPDUs stop; shown as *LOOP_Inc and cleared when BPDUs return.
A port shut down by the switch (for example by BPDU guard); it stays down until bounced or errdisable recovery acts.

summary: Loops cause broadcast storms, MAC table instability and duplicate frames; STP blocks ports to leave one active path.
Lowest bridge ID wins root: priority plus VLAN, then MAC. root primary sets 24576 (or 4096 below the root), root secondary 28672.
Root port: lowest root cost on each non-root switch. Designated port: one per link. The rest are alternate and discard.
Rapid PVST+ runs RSTP per VLAN: discarding, learning, forwarding, converging in about a second.
PortFast plus BPDU guard on access ports, root guard on designated downlinks, loop guard on root and alternate ports.
BKN* with ROOT_Inc or LOOP_Inc recovers by itself; a bpduguard err-disable needs shutdown and no shutdown.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a colleague how three switches in a triangle decide which switch is root and which single port blocks, using bridge ID and root cost, then explain where you would put PortFast, BPDU guard, root guard and loop guard and what each one prevents.

questions.question: Which three problems can a redundant switched network suffer without STP? (Choose three.)
choices: Broadcast storms
Routing loops between routers
MAC address table instability
Duplicate IP address conflicts
Hosts receiving multiple copies of the same frame
questions.explanation: The official guide lists broadcast storms, MAC table instability and multiple frame transmission. Routing loops are a Layer 3 problem, and duplicate IPs are an addressing mistake, not a loop symptom.

questions.question: How does STP remove loops from a redundant switched network?
choices: It disables the redundant cables at the physical layer
It places some ports in a blocking (discarding) state so one active path remains
It adds a TTL field to Ethernet frames
It routes frames between VLANs instead of switching them
questions.explanation: STP builds a loop-free tree by blocking selected ports. Blocked ports stay up and keep receiving BPDUs, so they can forward again if the active path fails.

questions.question: What is the default STP bridge priority on a Cisco switch, before the VLAN ID is added?
questions.explanation: The default priority is 32768. Show commands display it plus the VLAN ID, for example 32769 in VLAN 1.

questions.question: A switch uses the default priority. What priority value does show spanning-tree vlan 20 display in its Bridge ID?
questions.explanation: The extended system ID adds the VLAN number to the configured priority: 32768 + 20 = 32788.

questions.question: Which switch becomes the root bridge for VLAN 1?
choices: SW1
SW3, because it has the lowest MAC address
SW2, because it has the lowest priority
No root is elected until priorities match
questions.explanation: Priority is compared first, and SW2's 28673 is lowest, so its MAC is never compared. SW3's lower MAC would only matter if the priorities tied.

questions.question: Which value is accepted by spanning-tree vlan 10 priority?
questions.explanation: The priority must be a multiple of 4096 from 0 to 61440, because the low 12 bits hold the VLAN ID. 8192 is 2 x 4096; the others are not multiples of 4096.

questions.question: Type the global command that makes this switch the root bridge for VLAN 10 using Cisco's macro rather than a numeric priority.
questions.explanation: root primary picks 24576, or 4096 less than the current root's priority if needed, and stores the result as spanning-tree vlan 10 priority.

questions.question: After spanning-tree vlan 30 root secondary, which priority does the switch use for VLAN 30 (before adding the VLAN ID)?
questions.explanation: root secondary always sets 28672: lower than the default 32768 so it wins if the primary fails, but higher than the 24576 typically set by root primary.

questions.question: Match each link speed to its default Cisco STP port cost (short method).
questions.explanation: These are the original IEEE values that Cisco uses by default. The cost follows the speed the port is actually running at.

questions.question: SW4 receives Hellos on two ports. On Gi0/1 (port cost 4) the Hello lists a root cost of 8. On Fa0/1 (port cost 19) the Hello comes straight from the root with a root cost of 0. Which is SW4's root port, and what is its root cost?
choices: Fa0/1, root cost 19
Fa0/1, because it hears the root directly
Gi0/1, root cost 12
Gi0/1, root cost 4
questions.explanation: Gi0/1 totals 8 + 4 = 12 and Fa0/1 totals 0 + 19 = 19, so Gi0/1 wins with root cost 12. A direct link to the root is not automatically best; the lowest total cost is.

questions.question: Put the criteria a switch uses to choose its root port in order, from first to last tiebreaker.
questions.explanation: Root cost decides almost every case. If two paths tie, the switch prefers the neighbor with the lower bridge ID, and only parallel links to the same neighbor need the port priority and port number tiebreakers.

questions.question: Two non-root switches share a link, and both advertise the same root cost onto it. Which port becomes the designated port for that link?
choices: The port on the switch with the lower bridge ID
The port on the switch with the higher MAC address
Both ports become designated
The port with the lower port number, on either switch
questions.explanation: The designated port is chosen by lowest advertised root cost, and a tie goes to the lower bridge ID. The other switch's port becomes an alternate port.

questions.question: Which three are RSTP port states? (Choose three.)
choices: Discarding
Listening
Learning
Blocking
Forwarding
questions.explanation: RSTP uses discarding, learning and forwarding. Listening and blocking are 802.1D states; RSTP folds blocking (and disabled) into discarding and drops listening.

questions.question: Match each Rapid PVST+ port role or type to its description.

pairs.right: Best path from a non-root switch to the root
The forwarding port for a link
Discarding backup path to the root
Backup for a designated port on a shared segment
PortFast port facing an end device

questions.explanation: Root and designated ports forward. Alternate and backup ports discard but are ready to take over, and edge ports skip straight to forwarding.

questions.question: Type the global command that sets a switch to run Rapid PVST+.
questions.explanation: spanning-tree mode accepts pvst, rapid-pvst and mst. rapid-pvst runs RSTP separately for each VLAN.

questions.question: With default timers, how many seconds is the 802.1D forward delay?
questions.explanation: Forward delay is 15 seconds, spent once in listening and once in learning. Hello is 2 seconds and MaxAge is 20 seconds.

questions.question: Why can Rapid PVST+ move an alternate port to forwarding almost immediately when the root port fails?
choices: RSTP sets the forward delay to zero on every port
The alternate port was already forwarding traffic
RSTP disables MAC learning during convergence
The alternate port already receives Hellos from the same root, so RSTP knows it is a loop-free replacement path
questions.explanation: An alternate port hears the same root as the root port, so taking it over cannot create a loop and RSTP can move it straight to forwarding without timers. It was discarding until then.

questions.question: What is a benefit of running a separate spanning tree per VLAN with Rapid PVST+?
choices: Different VLANs can have different root bridges, so redundant uplinks each forward for some VLANs
It removes the need for BPDUs on trunks
Per-VLAN trees never need a root bridge
It allows loops in VLANs with few hosts
questions.explanation: With one tree per VLAN you can make SW1 root for some VLANs and SW2 root for others, so a link that blocks in one VLAN forwards in another and both uplinks carry traffic.

questions.question: Based on this output from SW3, which statement is correct?
questions.code:
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10

VLAN0010
  Spanning tree enabled protocol rstp
  Root ID    Priority    24586
             Address     0019.e859.5380
             Cost        19
             Port        1 (FastEthernet0/1)
             Hello Time   2 sec  Max Age 20 sec  Forward Delay 15 sec

  Bridge ID  Priority    28682  (priority 28672 sys-id-ext 10)
             Address     0019.e811.0a00
! lines omitted

Interface           Role Sts Cost      Prio.Nbr Type
------------------- ---- --- --------- -------- --------------------------------
Fa0/1               Root FWD 19        128.1    P2p
Gi0/1               Desg FWD 4         128.25   P2p
Gi0/2               Altn BLK 4         128.26   P2p
choices: SW3 is the root bridge for VLAN 10
SW3 is not the root; it reaches the root through Fa0/1 with cost 19 and is likely configured as root secondary
Gi0/2 is a backup port that forwards traffic
SW3's priority was configured as 28682
questions.explanation: The Root ID MAC differs from SW3's own MAC and lists a cost and root port, so SW3 is not root. Its configured priority is 28672 (28682 minus VLAN 10), the value root secondary sets. Gi0/2 is an alternate port that discards.

questions.question: In show spanning-tree, a port line reads 'Gi0/2  Altn BLK 4  128.26  P2p'. What is the port priority? (Number only.)
questions.explanation: Prio.Nbr shows port priority, then port number. 128 is the default port priority and 26 is the port number.

questions.question: Type the command that shows the spanning tree for VLAN 10 only.
questions.explanation: show spanning-tree vlan 10 lists the Root ID, Bridge ID and every port's role, state, cost and type in that VLAN's tree.

questions.question: Where should PortFast be enabled?
choices: On trunks between distribution switches
On the root bridge's uplinks
On access ports connected to end devices such as PCs and printers
On every port, to speed up convergence
questions.explanation: PortFast is for ports that cannot create a loop because they connect a single end device. On switch-to-switch links it bypasses the checks that prevent loops.

questions.question: Type the interface command that enables PortFast on an access port.
questions.explanation: spanning-tree portfast (spanning-tree portfast edge on newer IOS) makes the port an edge port that forwards immediately.

questions.question: spanning-tree portfast default is configured globally. Which ports use PortFast?
choices: Every port, including trunks
Only ports that also have spanning-tree portfast configured
All ports operating as access ports, unless disabled per port
Only ports in VLAN 1
questions.explanation: The global default applies to non-trunking (access) ports. A port can opt out with spanning-tree portfast disable, and trunks need spanning-tree portfast trunk explicitly.

questions.question: Type the interface command that enables BPDU guard on a port.
questions.explanation: spanning-tree bpduguard enable err-disables the port as soon as a BPDU arrives. It is the usual partner of PortFast on access ports.

questions.question: Fa0/5 was err-disabled by BPDU guard, and the rogue switch has been removed. No errdisable recovery is configured. What brings the port back?
questions.code: %PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Fa0/5, putting Fa0/5 in err-disable state
choices: Entering shutdown and then no shutdown on Fa0/5
Waiting for the BPDU holdtime to expire
Entering spanning-tree portfast on Fa0/5 again
Clearing the MAC address table
questions.explanation: An err-disabled port stays down until bounced manually, or until errdisable recovery cause bpduguard brings it back after the recovery interval (300 seconds by default).

questions.question: What is the effect of spanning-tree bpdufilter enable configured on an interface?
choices: The port err-disables when it receives a BPDU
The port loses PortFast when it receives a BPDU
The port accepts BPDUs only from the root bridge
The port stops sending and ignores received BPDUs, effectively disabling STP on it
questions.explanation: Interface-level BPDU filter suppresses BPDUs in both directions, so STP cannot detect a loop through that port. Losing PortFast on a received BPDU describes the global bpdufilter default form, and err-disabling describes BPDU guard.

questions.question: Type the global command that enables BPDU guard on every PortFast-enabled port.
questions.explanation: The global form applies BPDU guard to all ports operating as PortFast edge ports, which saves configuring it on every access port.

questions.question: Which two statements about root guard are true? (Choose two.)
choices: It puts the port in a root-inconsistent state when a superior BPDU arrives
It err-disables the port until an administrator intervenes
It recovers automatically when the superior BPDUs stop
It belongs on the switch's root port
It is enabled with spanning-tree bpduguard enable
questions.explanation: Root guard blocks the port (root-inconsistent) only while superior BPDUs keep arriving and then recovers on its own. It goes on designated ports facing downstream, and it is configured with spanning-tree guard root.

questions.question: A fiber link between SW1 and SW2 fails so that frames flow only from SW2 to SW1. SW2's alternate port on that link stops receiving BPDUs. Which feature prevents SW2 from moving that port to forwarding and creating a loop?
choices: Root guard
BPDU guard
Loop guard
PortFast
questions.explanation: Loop guard watches root and alternate ports. When their BPDUs stop, it puts the port in loop-inconsistent (discarding) state instead of letting STP make it designated and forwarding.

questions.question: Match each feature to where it is normally configured.

pairs.right: PortFast access ports facing end devices
Designated ports toward switches that must never be root
Root and alternate ports on switch-to-switch links
Ports to single hosts that should forward immediately

questions.explanation: Edge features (PortFast, BPDU guard) go on host ports. Root guard protects the root's position from downstream, and loop guard protects ports that must keep hearing BPDUs.

questions.question: Type the interface command that enables root guard.
questions.explanation: spanning-tree guard root enables root guard on the interface. The same guard command with the loop keyword enables loop guard instead, so a port has one or the other.

questions.question: Right after this change, the uplink to the distribution switch went err-disabled. Why?
questions.code:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description Uplink to DSW1
 switchport mode trunk
 spanning-tree portfast trunk
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable
choices: spanning-tree portfast trunk is not a valid command
Trunks cannot run spanning tree
BPDU guard err-disabled the port because the distribution switch sends BPDUs on it
The description is too long for a trunk
questions.explanation: Switch-to-switch links always carry BPDUs, so BPDU guard trips at once. PortFast and BPDU guard belong on edge ports; remove both from this uplink.

questions.question: All switches use default priorities for VLAN 20 except SW3, which is root with priority 16384. What priority does spanning-tree vlan 20 root primary set on SW1?
questions.explanation: The current root is already below 24576, so root primary picks 4096 less than the root: 16384 minus 4096 is 12288. 24576 would lose to SW3, and 28672 is root secondary.

questions.question: show spanning-tree vlan 30 lists this switch's Bridge ID priority as 24606. What priority was configured for VLAN 30? (Number only.)
questions.explanation: The displayed priority is the configured priority plus the extended system ID (the VLAN number): 24606 minus 30 is 24576, the value root primary usually sets.

questions.question: DSW1 is root primary for VLAN 10 and root secondary for VLAN 20; DSW2 is the reverse. DSW1 loses power. Which switch becomes root for VLAN 10?
choices: DSW2
The access switch with the lowest MAC address
No switch until DSW1 returns
Every switch becomes root for its own VLAN 10
questions.explanation: DSW2 holds 28672 for VLAN 10 (root secondary), lower than every default switch at 32768, so it wins the new election. It was already root for VLAN 20.

questions.question: Which three statements describe Rapid PVST+ BPDUs? (Choose three.)
choices: One set of BPDUs is sent for each VLAN
All VLANs share a single set of untagged BPDUs
BPDUs for a VLAN travel inside that VLAN, tagged on trunks
They are sent to the IEEE address 0180.C200.0000 only
The VLAN ID appears in the bridge ID's system ID extension
questions.explanation: Rapid PVST+ runs a separate instance per VLAN, so it sends BPDUs per VLAN, tagged with that VLAN on trunks, to Cisco multicast 0100.0CCC.CCCD, with the VLAN ID in the system ID extension. A single untagged set to 0180.C200.0000 describes standard IEEE RSTP.

questions.question: DSW1 is the intended root for VLAN 10. Based on this output from DSW1, what happened on Gi0/1?
questions.code:
DSW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10 | begin Interface
Interface           Role Sts Cost      Prio.Nbr Type
------------------- ---- --- --------- -------- --------------------------------
Gi0/1               Desg BKN*4         128.1    P2p *ROOT_Inc
Gi0/2               Desg FWD 4         128.2    P2p

%SPANTREE-2-ROOTGUARD_BLOCK: Root guard blocking port GigabitEthernet0/1 on VLAN0010.
choices: BPDU guard err-disabled Gi0/1 because a host sent BPDUs
Loop guard blocked Gi0/1 because BPDUs stopped arriving
Root guard blocked Gi0/1 because a device behind it claimed to be a better root
Gi0/1 is an alternate port waiting to become root port
questions.explanation: BKN* with *ROOT_Inc means root guard on Gi0/1 received a BPDU advertising a better root, probably from a newly connected switch with a low priority, and is blocking the port to protect the current root. The port recovers on its own when the superior BPDUs stop.

questions.question: Based on this output, which statement is true?
questions.code:
SW1# show spanning-tree summary
Switch is in rapid-pvst mode
Root bridge for: none
EtherChannel misconfig guard            is enabled
Extended system ID                      is enabled
Portfast Default                        is enabled
PortFast BPDU Guard Default             is enabled
Portfast BPDU Filter Default            is disabled
Loopguard Default                       is disabled
choices: Loop guard protects every port by default
PortFast ports err-disable if they receive a BPDU
BPDU filter is enabled globally on PortFast ports
SW1 is the root bridge for every VLAN
questions.explanation: The summary shows PortFast enabled by default on access ports and BPDU guard enabled by default on PortFast ports, while BPDU filter and loop guard defaults are off. The switch runs Rapid PVST+.

questions.question: Type the global command that enables loop guard on all point-to-point ports by default.
questions.explanation: spanning-tree loopguard default turns loop guard on globally; spanning-tree guard loop does the same on one interface.

questions.question: A user plugs a small switch into a PortFast port that has BPDU guard. Put the events in order.
items: The small switch sends a BPDU into the access port
BPDU guard sees the BPDU on the PortFast port
The switch err-disables the port and logs the event
An administrator removes the small switch
The administrator enters shutdown and no shutdown on the port
questions.explanation: BPDU guard acts on the first BPDU, err-disables the port and logs it. The port stays down until someone removes the cause and bounces the port (or errdisable recovery does it).

questions.question: SW2's Gi0/2 is normally an alternate port toward SW1. One strand of the fiber between them failed. Based on the output, which statement is correct?
questions.code:
SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 10 | begin Interface
Interface           Role Sts Cost      Prio.Nbr Type
------------------- ---- --- --------- -------- --------------------------------
Gi0/1               Root FWD 4         128.1    P2p
Gi0/2               Altn BKN*4         128.2    P2p *LOOP_Inc

%SPANTREE-2-LOOPGUARD_BLOCK: Loop guard blocking port GigabitEthernet0/2 on VLAN0010.
choices: Loop guard is keeping Gi0/2 blocked because its BPDUs stopped; it recovers when BPDUs return
Gi0/2 is err-disabled and must be bounced manually
Root guard blocked Gi0/2 because SW1 became root
Gi0/2 lost PortFast because it received a BPDU
questions.explanation: LOOP_Inc means loop guard noticed BPDUs stopped arriving on this alternate port and kept it blocking instead of letting it become designated and forwarding, which would create a loop over the one-way link. It unblocks automatically when BPDUs return.

questions.question: Match each spanning tree state or message to its cause.

pairs.right: Superior BPDU on a root guard port
BPDUs stopped on a loop guard port
Native VLAN differs on the two trunk ends
Any BPDU on a BPDU guard port

questions.explanation: Root guard and loop guard mark ports inconsistent and recover automatically; the PVID check catches native VLAN mismatches; BPDU guard err-disables.

questions.question: In show spanning-tree output, a port's Type column reads P2p Edge. What does Edge mean?
choices: The port connects to the root bridge
The port is blocked at the edge of the tree
The port uses half duplex
PortFast is enabled, so it is an edge port to an end device
questions.explanation: Edge marks an RSTP edge port, which on Cisco switches means PortFast is enabled: the port connects an end device and moves straight to forwarding. P2p means a full-duplex point-to-point link.
